newsitem.title: USA: Clinton leads Dole by double digits - Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton leads Dole by double digits - Reuters poll.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton regained a double-digit lead over Republican Bob Dole in the latest Reuters daily tracking poll released on Monday.
Clinton led with 46.6 percent to Dole's 35.8 percent. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot scored 4.9 percent and 10.6 percent remained undecided.

The poll, conducted by John Zogby Group International, tracks about 900 likely voters over a three-day period. The latest result, with a 3.3 percentage point margin of error, reflects polling Friday through Sunday.

The poll had showed a brief upsurge for Dole late last week following the second presidential debate. But his revival was brief and Clinton was again stretching his lead with two weeks left until Election Day on Nov 5.
"Significantly, the numbers of undecideds are dropping and they appear at this point to be breaking toward the president," said pollster John Zogby.

U.S. elections are really 51 separate contests in each of the states and the District of Columbia, with the winner in each state gaining delegates to the Electoral College, where a bare majority of 270 votes is needed to be elected.

In state-by-state polls, Clinton's lead over Dole appears impregnable. A survey by ABC television showed him leading in 30 states with 350 electoral votes. Dole led in 13 with 107 votes and eight states with 81 votes were rated close or even.

A 10-point victory for Clinton would translate into an overwhelming margin in the Electoral College. In the 1988 presidential election, Republican George Bush won by eight points and took 426 of the 538 electoral votes.
In the Reuters poll, Republicans had almost erased a Democratic lead when voters were asked which candidate they would support in their congressional district.

And in a separate but related question on which party they would prefer to control Congress, sentiment had shifted markedly in favour of the Republicans despite Democrat Clinton's hopes of ending their majority in one or both houses.
In the latest Zogby, voters said they favoured Republicans by almost six points in the Senate and three-and-a-half points for the House.
